extracted.intended_audience: agency web designers, agency officials responsible for rulemaking outreach, and policymakers concerned with public participation in rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing federal (or agency) websites so that rulemaking information and opportunities for public comment are discoverable and usable by ordinary citizens, not only frequent or sophisticated users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design websites with rulemaking participation in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should design their websites with rulemaking participation by the general public in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Website design decisions should explicitly consider rulemaking as a purpose (not merely rely on overall traffic/use data). Treat making rulemaking information accessible as an objective in site design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence of rulemaking information on the home page
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking information should be listed prominently on the home page rather than buried in low-visibility menus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hiding 'rulemaking' or 'regulation' in deep pull-downs or under unrelated headings. Example anti-pattern: putting a primary link to rulemaking under a tab labeled 'Business and Licensing' so ordinary citizens are unlikely to find it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely exclusively on 'top tasks' or traffic metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclusive focus on current website use or demand (the 'top tasks' approach) will likely push rulemaking information far into the background because rulemaking traffic is typically low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Site prioritization should weigh democratic importance of rulemaking (binding law with penalties) alongside traffic data; rulemaking merits prominence even if not a 'top task' by usage statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality across user types; accessibility to less sophisticated users
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites should be neutral across user types and more accessible to less sophisticated or one-shot participants, not designed only for frequent/familiar users (e.g., businesses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should accommodate one-time users and laypersons by avoiding jargon, opaque navigation, and assumptions about prior knowledge. Prioritize discoverability and straightforward pathways for novice users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide prominent, easy access point for filing public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Websites should offer a clear and prominent access point for comments (e.g., an obvious 'Take Action' or 'File a Public Comment' flow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that 'file a comment' links are visible and accompanied by contextual information that helps a lay user know what they are commenting on and how to do so meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include informative summaries for listed proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings listed on the site (e.g., 'Most Active Proceedings') should include summaries or descriptive accounts that help ordinary citizens understand the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summaries should include high-level descriptions, deadlines, applicable standards for agency decisions, and links to supporting materials. Anti-pattern: listings with no description or misleading/insufficient labeling (e.g., showing completed proceedings without indicating status).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly label the type and status of proceedings (rulemaking vs. non-rulemaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Users should be able to tell from listings whether a proceeding is a rulemaking and what its current status is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an item appears among rulemaking-related lists, explicitly state whether it is a rulemaking or some other proceeding, and indicate deadlines and stages so the public can assess relevance and opportunities to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure lists of proposed rules and proceedings are complete and up-to-date
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency sites should provide complete and current lists of the agency’s proposed rules and active proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid incomplete lists or stale entries; make clear which items are current, which are completed, and provide timely updates. Example problem: 'Most Active Proceedings' including largely or fully completed matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide direct links to notices and supporting documents from summary/listing pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Listings and summaries should link to the underlying notices, documents, and supporting materials so users can access primary sources easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While search pages may contain all documents, users benefit from direct links on the summary or listing pages rather than needing to search by proceeding number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming user familiarity; provide layperson-friendly context
rubrics_metrics.description: Site content should not assume prior knowledge; provide context sufficient for ordinary citizens to understand what a proceeding is about and how it affects them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain-language descriptions, explain technical terms or institutional labels, and include short contextual notes (e.g., why the proceeding matters, who is affected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design both search functionality and curated, human-readable summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Search tools alone are insufficient; agencies should combine robust search with curated summaries and navigation tailored to non-expert users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search can help power users locate documents, but ordinary citizens also need curated entry points and readable summaries on pages they encounter without extensive searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for statutory and executive directives about public participation when making design choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Website design decisions should give due consideration to the values of public participation reflected in laws and executive orders calling on agencies to use electronic media to enhance public understanding and role in rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers and officials should treat legal/ethical obligations to facilitate participation as constraints or goals in site design, not optional extras to be overridden by traffic-driven priorities.
